extracted.intended_audience: ML/AI researchers, conference organizers, peer-review policy makers, and researchers studying peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluation framework for using (and deciding whether to deploy) AI systems for scholarly peer review, including empirical metrics, user-study questions, policy recommendations, and measurement/robustness checks. Targets conference peer review workflows and empirical studies of AI-assisted reviewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-driven requirements and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing and updating requirements for acceptable AI use in peer review should be a deliberate, community-driven process, not an afterthought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The need for explicit community deliberation about peer review values and automation boundaries; what is 'not yet acceptable' today may become acceptable as accuracy improves if it meets community-defined requirements (Yang, 2025). Policy-setting should be transparent and regulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: User studies on human-AI interaction in reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Before deploying AI tools for reviewing, conduct user studies to understand how AI assistance changes reviewer behavior (e.g., overreliance, hivemind effects, catching or propagating AI errors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate questions such as: How does AI assistance affect diversity of reviewer opinions? Do reviewers catch AI errors or propagate them? What interface designs promote engagement and critical thinking rather than passive acceptance? How can organizers enforce AI-usage policies? Cite human-AI interaction literature (Buçinca et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2025). The goal: tools that accelerate human review without deteriorating quality or collapsing opinion plurality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rethink incentive structures to value human reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: Address undervaluation of human reviewing by making human expertise more valuable instead of replacing reviewers with cheaper automated alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Current incentives lead to rushed reviews and declining quality; invest in reviewer incentives to improve human input (Kim et al., 2025b). Maximize human expert input at process stages AI is not fit to automate without oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve diversity/plurality of opinions (avoid hivemind effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI reviewing systems must not collapse reviewer outputs into highly similar, homogeneous opinions across and within papers (the 'hivemind effect').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper documents that AI reviewers produce far more similar outputs than humans, undermining peer review's purpose to aggregate diverse judgments. Evaluation should measure both within-paper agreement and cross-paper similarity (IntraSim and InterSim) and ensure AI similarity is comparable to human baselines rather than substantially higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive validity for final decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer scores (AI or human) should be informative predictors of final acceptance decisions; AI scores should achieve predictive validity comparable to human reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured with metrics like AUC: in the paper, averaged human scores predicted acceptance with AUC=0.822 vs. averaged AI scores AUC=0.710 on matched papers. Use similar predictive-validity analyses when evaluating AI reviewers; poor predictive validity is a serious practical consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to gaming (robustness to paper laundering)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI reviewing systems must be robust to simple automated rewrites ('paper laundering') that artificially boost scores without substantive scientific improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define and test laundering attacks: zero-shot automated rewrites that alter style/phrasing and can increase AI reviewer scores. Evaluate via controlled launderer models and prompts; measure frequency and magnitude of score increases vs decreases across conditions. Documented failure mode: laundering often adds stylistic confidence or fabricated sections that inflate scores while not improving content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low templated/boilerplate reuse across papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Good reviews should avoid high reuse of identical long template phrases across many different papers; high template-phrase coverage indicates spurious agreement and lack of paper-specific critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure n-gram template reuse (6–25 word phrases) and report per-reviewer-type coverage. Example: GPT-5.1 reviewer reused top phrases across 13.3% of papers while human ICLR reviewers show <1% reuse. Aim for template reuse rates close to human baselines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argumentative diversity (not just linguistic diversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity metrics should capture diversity of viewpoints, arguments, and evaluative stances, not only linguistic/semantic surface similarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embedding-based similarity metrics capture linguistic/semantic patterns but do not directly measure argumentative diversity or information gain. Develop or apply metrics that assess argumentative content (e.g., novelty of critiques, distinct evaluative stances) and quantify information contributed by additional reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus evaluation on substantive critique sections
rubrics_metrics.description: When measuring reviewer similarity or diversity, emphasize weaknesses and questions sections where critique is most directly expressed rather than boilerplate summary/strengths text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper shows that restricting analyses to weaknesses and questions increases the measured hivemind effect for AI and reduces human boilerplate influence. Use targeted-section analyses to assess substantive convergence vs superficial similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validate AI-generation / detection labels with independent signals
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying AI-generated reviews in the wild, validate detection labels (e.g., Pangram) using independent human-sourced evidence like author complaints and manual verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example validation: of 58 author-accused reviews, 86.2% were flagged by Pangram as fully AI-generated; use multiple complementary validation strategies because detection labels can contain classification errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate robustness across prompts, models, and settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess AI reviewer behavior and associated failures across diverse prompts, model versions, temperatures, and launderer/reviewer model combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controlled experiments should vary prompts, launderers, reviewer models; in the paper, simulations used a single prompt and two models, a limitation acknowledged. Robust evaluation must account for experimental homogeneity possibly under- or over-stating effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for confounds such as review length
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether measured similarity or other effects are explained by confounds (e.g., review length) and re-run analyses within overlapping length ranges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports AI reviews being longer (507 vs 424 words) but shows the hivemind effect persists after restricting to overlapping length ranges (261–672 words). Report length statistics and test correlations between length and similarity (weak correlations |r|<0.13 here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intra- and inter-reviewer similarity metrics (IntraSim, InterSim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify within-paper agreement (IntraSim) and cross-paper similarity (InterSim) to characterize AI vs human reviewer homogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute embedding-based similarity metrics over review text (optionally restricted to critique sections). Report effect sizes (Cohen's d), tests of statistical significance, and stratify by subfield/area. Example reported AI-AI InterSim increases of ~0.49 vs human ~0.47 in samples; report these comparisons with sample sizes and p-values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report reviewer-score correlations and statistical properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure Pearson correlations between reviewer scores (AI-AI, AI-human, human-human) and report p-values and sample sizes to compare consistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: AI-AI (GPT vs Claude) r=0.492; human-human r=0.137 in sample. Interpret cautiously when sample sizes are small (n=60 in simulation). Use correlations alongside predictive-validity metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical pre-deployment evaluation and a 'science of peer review automation'
rubrics_metrics.description: Require rigorous empirical evaluations of tools before deployment, including experiments, user studies, robustness tests, and ongoing monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors call for transparent science that empirically evaluates tools before deployment, studies human-AI interactions, and develops incentive structures. Deployment should follow validated evidence that tools do not degrade review quality or plurality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability, democratic legitimacy, and measurement validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond technical performance, consider accountability mechanisms, democratic legitimacy of decisions, and validity of measurements used to justify automation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meeting technical necessary conditions alone does not justify full automation. Questions of who is accountable, how decisions are legitimated within the community, and whether measurements reflect meaningful aspects of review quality must be deliberated publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interface and policy design to avoid overreliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Design reviewer interfaces and organizational policies to reduce cognitive overreliance on AI suggestions and to promote critical engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite interventions like cognitive forcing functions (Buçinca et al., 2021). Interface design research should test which UX elements promote independent judgment. Organizers should specify and enforce AI-usage policies (e.g., conservative prohibitions used at some venues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent documentation of automated procedures (implementation details)
rubrics_metrics.description: When conducting AI-review experiments or deploying tools, document implementation details (models, prompts, preprocessing, launderer pipeline) so results are reproducible and attack vectors are clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix B provides an example: model names, prompt sources, LaTeX preprocessing, extraction delimiters, and how rewritten content and generated citations are handled. Transparent documentation enables community scrutiny and robustness checks.
